title: General Data Protection Regulation — Regulation (EU) 2016/679
summary: The EU's general data-protection law, published in the OJ on 4 May 2016 and applicable from 25 May 2018; Arts. 5, 6, 9, 22 and 35 are the main GDPR hooks used against AI training, profiling and automated decision-making.

title: Digital Services Act — Regulation (EU) 2022/2065
summary: Sets due-diligence, content-moderation and systemic-risk duties for online intermediaries and very large online platforms; published in the OJ on 27 October 2022, applicable from 17 February 2024. It is the legal basis for the Commission's DSA proceedings against X/Grok.

title: European AI Office established — Commission Decision C/2024/1459
summary: Establishes the European AI Office within DG CNECT to implement and enforce the AI Act, especially the rules for general-purpose AI models. Decision of 24 January 2024, published in the OJ on 14 February 2024, in force 21 February 2024.
notes: Decision of 24 January 2024, published in the OJ on 14 February 2024.

title: EU AI Act — Regulation (EU) 2024/1689
summary: The world's first comprehensive AI law: risk-based rules for AI systems, prohibitions, high-risk obligations, GPAI duties and transparency duties. Adopted 13 June 2024, published in the OJ on 12 July 2024, in force 1 August 2024.
next_milestone: 2 Dec 2027: high-risk duties begin (Annex III stand-alone systems)
notes: Adopted 13 June 2024.

title: EDPB Opinion 28/2024 on AI models and personal data
summary: EDPB opinion (requested by the Irish DPC) on when an AI model trained on personal data can be considered anonymous, when legitimate interest is a lawful basis for training/deployment, and the consequences of unlawful training data.
notes: Requested by the Irish DPC.

title: Commission Guidelines on prohibited AI practices (Art. 5 AI Act)
summary: Non-binding Commission guidelines interpreting the eight prohibited AI practices (manipulation, exploitation of vulnerabilities, social scoring, crime-risk prediction, untargeted facial scraping, emotion recognition, biometric categorisation, real-time remote biometric identification). The prohibitions applied from 2 February 2025.
source_title: European Commission, Guidelines on prohibited AI practices (C(2025) 884 final, published 4 Feb 2025; formally adopted as C(2025) 5052 final, 29 Jul 2025)
notes: The prohibitions applied from 2 February 2025. Content approved 4 Feb 2025 as C(2025) 884 final; formally adopted 29 Jul 2025 as C(2025) 5052 final.

title: General-Purpose AI Code of Practice
summary: Voluntary code drawn up by 13 independent experts with ~1,000 stakeholders, in three chapters (Transparency, Copyright, Safety and Security), to help GPAI providers demonstrate compliance with Arts. 53 and 55 AI Act. Confirmed by the Commission and AI Board as an adequate voluntary compliance tool.
notes: Drawn up by 13 independent experts with ~1,000 stakeholders; three chapters (Transparency, Copyright, Safety and Security).

title: Digital Omnibus on AI — Regulation (EU) 2026/1744
summary: Amends the AI Act to simplify implementation: postpones high-risk application dates (2 Dec 2027 for stand-alone Annex III systems; 2 Aug 2028 for Annex I product-embedded systems), narrows some duties, and adds two new prohibited practices (Art. 5(1)(ba)–(bb)): AI systems generating non-consensual intimate material and child sexual abuse material, applicable from 2 Dec 2026. Published in the OJ 24 July 2026, in force 27 July 2026.
next_milestone: 2 Dec 2026: new Art. 5 prohibitions (ba)–(bb) apply; 2 Dec 2027: high-risk duties begin (Annex III stand-alone systems); 2 Aug 2028: Annex I product-embedded systems
notes: Published in the OJ 24 July 2026.

title: France — National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence
summary: Launched March 2018 following the Villani report; €1,527m public funding for 2018–2022 across research, higher education, public transformation, economy and defence/security, with an acceleration phase announced November 2021 for 2022–2025.
source_title: Ministère de l'Économie, Stratégie nationale pour l'IA, 2e phase — dossier de presse, 8 Nov 2021
notes: Following the Villani report; €1,527m public funding for 2018–2022; acceleration phase announced November 2021 for 2022–2025.

title: Germany — AI Strategy of the Federal Government
summary: Federal strategy adopted 15 November 2018 and updated 2 December 2020, aiming for competitive, human-centric and trustworthy "AI made in Germany"; initial €3bn to 2025, raised to ~€5bn in the 2020 update, which added pandemic, sustainability and health priorities.
source_title: Die Bundesregierung, Strategie Künstliche Intelligenz — Fortschreibung 2020 (Dec 2020)
notes: Updated 2 December 2020; initial €3bn to 2025, raised to ~€5bn in the 2020 update.

title: Denmark — National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence
summary: Government strategy (Ministry of Finance and Ministry of Industry, Business and Financial Affairs), March 2019, aiming to make Denmark a front-runner in responsible AI use, with four objectives (ethical human-centric basis, research, business growth, world-class public services) and 24 initiatives.
notes: Four objectives and 24 initiatives.

title: Netherlands — Strategic Action Plan for Artificial Intelligence (SAPAI)
summary: Government of the Netherlands action plan built on three pillars: capitalising on societal/economic opportunities, creating the right conditions (education, research, data, connectivity), and strengthening foundations (public values, human rights, trust and safety).
source_title: Tweede Kamer, Parliamentary Papers blg-903667 (SAPAI report)
notes: Three pillars: opportunities, conditions, foundations.

title: Poland — Policy for the Development of Artificial Intelligence in Poland from 2020
summary: Council of Ministers Resolution No. 196 of 28 December 2020 (Monitor Polski 2021, item 23) setting short-, medium- and long-term AI goals across six areas: society, innovative companies, science, education, international cooperation and the public sector.
notes: Council of Ministers Resolution No. 196 of 28 December 2020.

title: Ireland — National AI Strategy, "AI – Here for Good"
summary: Ireland's first national AI strategy, launched 8 July 2021 by the Taoiseach and the Department of Enterprise, Trade and Employment; a whole-of-government roadmap for trustworthy, human-centric AI adoption in enterprise and public services, refreshed in November 2024.
notes: Refreshed in November 2024.

title: Spain — AESIA created, Royal Decree 729/2023
summary: Royal Decree 729/2023 of 22 August 2023 approves the statute of the Agencia Española de Supervisión de la Inteligencia Artificial (AESIA), based in A Coruña — the first EU member-state AI supervision agency, later Spain's AI market-surveillance authority and single point of contact. Published in the BOE on 2 September 2023.
notes: Published in the BOE on 2 September 2023; based in A Coruña; Spain's AI market-surveillance authority and single point of contact.

title: Spain — Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2024
summary: Council of Ministers approval on 14 May 2024 of the updated AI strategy (continuing the 2020 ENIA), structured in three axes and eight levers — supercomputing, Spanish/co-official-language models (ALIA), public- and private-sector uptake, and transparent, ethical, humanistic AI — with €1.5bn for 2024–2025.
notes: Continuing the 2020 ENIA; €1.5bn for 2024–2025.

title: Italy — AI Law, Legge 23 settembre 2025, n. 132
summary: Italy's comprehensive national AI law ("Disposizioni e deleghe al Governo in materia di intelligenza artificiale"), the first such law in the EU; it sets a biennial national AI strategy, designates AgID and the National Cybersecurity Agency (ACN) as national AI authorities, and adds AI-related criminal offences. Published in Gazzetta Ufficiale No. 223 on 25 September 2025, in force 10 October 2025.
notes: First comprehensive national AI law in the EU; in force 10 October 2025.

title: Spain — AI regulatory sandbox, Royal Decree 817/2023
summary: Royal Decree 817/2023 of 8 November 2023 creates the first EU AI regulatory sandbox, under the AI Act's sandbox provisions, for testing AI systems under regulatory supervision; published in the Boletín Oficial del Estado on 9 November 2023 (No. 268), in force 10 November 2023.
notes: BOE-A-2023-22767. Pilot: single call December 2024–January 2025; secondary reporting says the pilot concluded 1 July 2026 after supporting 25 organisations and producing 16 guides.

title: Germany — AI Act implementation act (KI-MIG), Gesetz zur Durchführung der Verordnung (EU) 2024/1689
summary: Germany's AI Act implementation act, adopted by the Bundestag on 11 June 2026 and promulgated on 22 July 2026 (BGBl. 2026 I Nr. 223), in force 29 July 2026. Article 1 is the KI-MIG (KI-Marktüberwachungs- und Innovationsförderungsgesetz), making the Federal Network Agency (Bundesnetzagentur) the central market surveillance authority, single point of contact and central complaints body; BaFin covers financial-sector AI, and an independent market surveillance chamber handles certain fundamental-rights-sensitive high-risk systems. The act also requires at least one AI regulatory sandbox and adds national fines of up to €50,000.
source_title: Springer, 'Enforcing the AI Act at the national level: Germany's KI-MIG as a blueprint?'
notes: Bundestag adopted 11 June 2026; Bundesrat declined to call the Mediation Committee 10 July 2026; BGBl. 2026 I Nr. 223 (issue of 28 July 2026). The Bundesnetzagentur's own press release of 29 July 2026 confirms entry into force; its direct URL returned 404 when checked on 23 Nov 2026, so the peer-reviewed article is cited as the source for now.

title: Italy — Legislative Decree 160/2026: police use of AI and AI liability
summary: Legislative Decree 160 of 9 September 2026, adopted under Law 132/2025, aligns national law with the AI Act on police use of AI systems and on civil and criminal liability: it creates a new Criminal Code offence (Art. 437-bis) for failing to adopt safety and human-oversight measures for high-risk AI (1–5 years' imprisonment) and extends civil and corporate liability (Legislative Decree 231/2001) to AI-related harm. Published in Gazzetta Ufficiale No. 214 on 15 September 2026, in force 30 September 2026.
notes: Code 26G00179; GU Serie Generale n. 214, 15 September 2026.

title: Italy — Legislative Decree 179/2026: national AI governance, market surveillance and sanctions
summary: Legislative Decree 179 of 7 October 2026, adopted under Law 132/2025, sets Italy's national AI governance: AgID as notifying authority, the National Cybersecurity Agency (ACN) as market surveillance authority, sectoral authorities, penalties of up to €35m or 7% of turnover for prohibited practices, regulatory sandboxes, AI literacy measures and rules on AI in employment. Published in Gazzetta Ufficiale No. 234 on 8 October 2026, in force 23 October 2026.
notes: GU No. 234, 8 October 2026.

title: Commission Guidelines on the implementation of the transparency obligations for certain AI systems under Article 50 AI Act
summary: Non-binding Commission Guidelines (C(2026) 5054, adopted 20 July 2026) on the AI Act's Article 50 transparency duties — machine-readable marking of AI-generated content, labelling of deepfakes and of AI-generated text on matters of public interest — issued under Art. 96(1)(d). Article 50 applies from 2 August 2026; generative systems placed on the market before that date have until 2 December 2026 to add machine-readable marking under Art. 50(2).
source_title: European Commission, Digital Strategy: Guidelines on AI transparency obligations
next_milestone: 2 Dec 2026: Art. 50(2) machine-readable marking due for pre-2 Aug 2026 generative systems

title: Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-Generated Content
summary: Voluntary Code of Practice published 10 June 2026 (press release IP/26/1328) to help providers and deployers demonstrate compliance with Article 50: Section 1 commits providers to marking AI-generated or manipulated content in a machine-readable way (metadata, watermarks, detection tools); Section 2 commits deployers to labelling deepfakes and AI-generated public-interest text. The Commission and the AI Board assessed it as an adequate voluntary compliance tool; about 190 organisations had signed by 31 July 2026.
source_title: European Commission, Digital Strategy: Code of Practice on marking and labelling AI-generated content
next_milestone: 2 Dec 2026: Art. 50(2) machine-readable marking due for pre-2 Aug 2026 generative systems
notes: Published 10 June 2026 (press release IP/26/1328); the 31 July 2026 date sometimes cited is the Commission's announcement that about 190 organisations had signed, not the publication date.

title: Finland — National AI strategy, 'Finland's Age of Artificial Intelligence'
issuer: Ministry of Economic Affairs and Employment (Finland)
summary: Finland's first national AI strategy, adopted 23 October 2017 by the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Employment, setting eight key actions to make Finland a leader in applying AI — covering business, public services, skills and the legal environment — and launching the national AI programme continued in the 2019 final report and the AI 4.0 programme.
source_title: Ministry of Economic Affairs and Employment (Finland), 'Finland's Age of Artificial Intelligence'
notes: Direct fetch of the source URL returned 403 (bot-blocked) on 23 Nov 2026; the record was verified via AIPolicyTracker, which cites this official source (verified 26 Sep 2026).

title: Estonia — National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2019–2021 (Kratt Strategy)
summary: Estonia's national AI strategy, adopted by the Cabinet in July 2019 on the proposals of an expert group led by the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Communications and the Government Office, with at least €10m for 2019–2021 to advance AI uptake in the public and private sectors, research and skills, and the legal environment; it underpins the 'Kratt' programme of reusable public-sector AI components and the Bürokratt virtual assistant.
source_title: European Commission, Interoperable Europe: Digital public services based on open source — Bürokratt
notes: Adopted at Cabinet meeting on 25 July 2019; a successor strategy covered 2022–2023.

title: Czechia — National Artificial Intelligence Strategy of the Czech Republic 2030
summary: Updated national AI strategy approved by the government (Resolution No. 520) on 24 July 2024, building on the 2019 National AI Strategy across seven key areas — research, development and innovation; education and expertise; skills; and AI in industry, services and public administration — to develop the Czech AI ecosystem while addressing the technology's challenges.
source_title: Ministry of Industry and Trade (Czechia), Artificial Intelligence
notes: Updates the 2019 National AI Strategy (approved 6 May 2019).

title: Austria — Artificial Intelligence Mission Austria 2030 (AIM AT 2030)
summary: Austria's national AI strategy, adopted by the Council of Ministers on 25 August 2021, pursuing three objectives — broad use of AI oriented to the common good and fundamental rights, Austria as a research and innovation location, and competitiveness of the Austrian technology and business location — with 13 fields of action covering trustworthy AI, data, infrastructure, skills, public administration and financing, plus an implementation plan added in 2024.
source_title: Federal Ministry for Climate Action, Environment, Energy, Mobility, Innovation and Technology (BMK), AIM AT 2030
notes: Complementary AI implementation plan (KI-Umsetzungsplan 2024) added in 2024.

title: Portugal — AI Portugal 2030, National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence
summary: Portugal's national AI strategy, launched in February 2019 under the INCoDe.2030 initiative and coordinated by the Foundation for Science and Technology (FCT), structured around five pillars — inclusion and education, qualification and specialisation, research and innovation, public administration modernisation, and ethics and safety — to strengthen AI capabilities in the public and private sectors.
source_title: OECD.AI: AI Portugal 2030 — National Strategy for AI
notes: Succeeded by the National Artificial Intelligence Agenda 2026–2030 (ANIA), approved by Council of Ministers Resolution 2/2026 of 8 January 2026 — to be verified against the Diário da República text in a later run.

title: Luxembourg — Artificial Intelligence: a Strategic Vision for Luxembourg
summary: Luxembourg's national AI strategy, published in May 2019 as part of the Digital Luxembourg programme, setting out a vision of human-centric AI based on an efficient and sustainable data-driven ecosystem, with seven pillars — Luxembourg as a living laboratory for applied AI, data, ethics and privacy, investment and strategic partnerships, AI for the public sector, skills and lifelong learning, and international cooperation.
source_title: Government of Luxembourg, 'Artificial Intelligence: a Strategic Vision for Luxembourg' (PDF)
notes: A comprehensive review concluded in May 2025; the 2025 'Accelerating Digital Sovereignty 2030' initiative now integrates AI with data and quantum strategies.
